headline: Burnham heads to Brussels on 20 November for second UK-EU summit on trade, energy and youth mobility

terms.meaning: The EU's shared trading area, where goods move without most border checks.
A scheme that puts a price on pollution so firms pay for the carbon they release.

levels.headline: Burnham heads to Brussels on 20 November for second UK-EU summit on trade, energy and youth mobility
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend the second UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November, where he is due to meet European Council president António Costa and European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen. The government says the aim is to cut costs and red tape for farmers and businesses.
In a Commons statement in October, Burnham listed the priorities: a food and drink trade deal, progress on linking emissions trading and energy systems, a youth experience scheme, and deeper cooperation on immigration. He called a good outcome his immediate priority, with a longer-term discussion on future options to follow.
Burnham has said the status quo with Brussels is not good enough and has floated closer options, including rejoining the customs union or Single Market, while ruling out Schengen and the euro. Reports say the carbon market link is expected to be announced, though critics warn it could raise costs for British industry. No outcome is known yet. Burnham became prime minister on 20 July after Keir Starmer resigned.
levels.why: The summit could change the rules on trade, energy costs and how people travel and work between the UK and the EU.

levels.headline: Burnham to attend second UK-EU summit on 20 November with food trade, carbon market and youth scheme on the table
levels.body:
Andy Burnham will travel to Brussels on 20 November for the second UK-EU summit, meeting António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen. Ministers say the goal is lower costs and less red tape for farmers and businesses.
The agenda he set out in the Commons includes a food and drink trade deal, links between the UK and EU carbon markets and energy systems, a youth experience scheme and closer cooperation on immigration. He says a good result now is his priority, with a wider conversation about the long-term relationship later.
Burnham says the current arrangement is not good enough. He has raised options such as rejoining the customs union or Single Market, but has ruled out joining Schengen or the euro. Some critics say linking carbon markets could push up costs for British industry. The outcome is not yet known. Burnham has been prime minister since 20 July.
levels.why: Decisions made in Brussels could affect food prices, energy bills and job and travel options for young people.

levels.headline: Burnham goes to Brussels on 20 November for talks on food, energy and young people's travel
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet the leaders of the European Council and European Commission in Brussels on 20 November. It is the second summit between the UK and the European Union since Brexit talks reset. The government wants to cut costs and paperwork for farmers and businesses.
He wants a deal making it easier to trade food and drink, plans to link the UK and EU systems that charge firms for carbon pollution, a scheme letting young people live and work abroad for a time, and more cooperation on immigration.
Burnham says the current situation is not good enough and has talked about closer ties in future, such as the customs union or Single Market. He has said no to the euro and to open Schengen borders. Critics worry the carbon link could raise costs for industry. No result is known yet.
levels.why: It affects what food costs, how easily firms can sell to Europe and what chances young people may get abroad.

levels.headline: UK and EU leaders to meet in Brussels on 20 November to try to cut trade red tape
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will go to Brussels on 20 November to meet the heads of the European Council and the European Commission. The government says the meeting aims to cut costs and red tape for farmers and businesses.
Topics include a food and drink trade deal, connecting the UK and EU carbon pricing schemes and energy systems, a youth experience scheme, and working together on immigration. Burnham says he wants a good outcome first and a longer talk about the future relationship afterwards.
He has said things as they stand are not good enough and has mentioned the customs union and Single Market as possible long-term options. He has ruled out the euro and Schengen, the EU's passport-free travel area. Some critics fear the carbon market link could make things dearer for British industry. Nobody knows the result yet.
levels.why: A deal could lower costs for firms and shoppers, but there are also worries about extra costs for industry.

levels.headline: Prime Minister to meet EU leaders in Brussels to talk about trade, energy and young people
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet two top EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November. The government says it wants to make life cheaper and simpler for farmers and businesses that sell goods to Europe.
He plans to talk about a deal on food and drink, joining up the way the UK and EU charge companies for the pollution they cause, a scheme for young people to spend time living and working abroad, and working together on immigration. He says he wants a good result from this meeting first.
Mr Burnham has said the current relationship is not good enough. He has mentioned bigger changes for later, such as closer trade rules, but he has said no to the euro and to the EU's passport-free zone. Some people worry that linking the carbon systems could raise costs for British industry. We do not yet know what will be agreed.
levels.why: The talks could make trade with Europe easier and may change what things cost.

levels.headline: The PM will meet EU leaders on 20 November to try to make trading with Europe easier
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is going to Brussels on 20 November. He will meet the leaders of the European Union's main bodies. Since Brexit, the UK has not been part of the EU, so trading with Europe has more forms and checks. The government wants to cut those costs.
The talks cover selling food and drink, linking the way both sides charge firms for polluting, a plan for young people to spend time abroad, and working together on immigration.
Mr Burnham says things are not good enough as they are. He may want closer ties later, but he says the UK will not join the euro or the EU's open-border travel zone. Some people say the pollution scheme could make costs higher for factories here. We do not know the result yet.
levels.why: It could make buying and selling goods across the Channel simpler and cheaper.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister will meet EU leaders to talk about trade
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is going to Brussels on 20 November. Brussels is where the European Union has its main offices. He will meet two of the EU's top leaders.
The UK left the EU a few years ago. Since then, selling things such as food to Europe has meant more forms and checks. The government wants to make that easier and cheaper for farmers and shops.
They will also talk about a plan to let young people live and work abroad for a while. And they will talk about pollution. Both sides charge companies money for polluting, and they may join those systems together.
Mr Burnham says things are not good enough now. He will not take the UK back into the euro, the EU's shared money. Nobody knows yet what will be agreed.
levels.why: What is agreed could change how easily Britain sells and buys things from Europe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister is going to talk with leaders in Europe
levels.body:
The Prime Minister is called Andy Burnham. On 20 November he is going to a city called Brussels. Leaders of the European Union work there. The EU is a group of countries in Europe that work together.
The UK used to be in that group, but it left. Now it is harder for UK farmers to sell their food to those countries. There are more forms to fill in. The Prime Minister wants to make this easier.
They will also talk about young people being able to live and work in another country for a short time. And they will talk about keeping the air clean.
The Prime Minister says things are not good enough now. We do not yet know what they will agree. We will find out after the meeting.
levels.why: It could make it easier and cheaper for people in different countries to trade and work together.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister visits friends across the sea
levels.body:
Imagine your school and the school across the road used to share a playground. Then one school said, we want our own. Now it is harder to share toys and games. Some people think that is a bit silly.
That is a little like the UK and the European Union. The UK used to be part of the group, then left. On 20 November, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, will meet the group's leaders. He wants to make it easier to share things again.
They will talk about selling food, about young people spending time in another country, and about cleaner air.
He says things are not good enough now. Nobody knows yet what they will decide. We will find out after they have met.
levels.why: Sometimes countries try to get along better so that people can share and trade more easily.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister is going to meet some leaders from other countries
levels.body:
Do you know that countries are a bit like big groups of friends? Our country is called the United Kingdom. Next door, across the sea, are lots of other countries. Many of them are in a team called the EU.
Our country used to be in that team, then it left. Since then, it has been a bit harder to send things like food across the sea. There are lots of forms to fill in, just like when you ask a teacher to sign lots of notes.
On 20 November the Prime Minister, whose name is Andy Burnham, will meet the leaders of that team. He wants to make things easier, so people can swap things and share.
We do not know yet what they will say. We will find out soon.
levels.why: It is about countries getting along and making it easier to share and trade.

headline: S&P 500 closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday, the last completed session, as Nvidia fell again

terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 of the largest companies listed in the US.
An index dominated by technology companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday, the last completed session, as Nvidia fell again
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday 13 November, the last completed trading session; US markets reopen on Monday. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.91% to 25,136.27, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to 52,347.55, according to CNBC.
Tech shares were hit as chipmaker Nvidia extended its recent losses after the exit of founder and chief executive Jensen Huang. Another data provider, Trading Economics, reported slightly different Nasdaq and Dow figures, so the CNBC numbers are used here.
Despite Friday's falls, CNBC said all three major indexes had their best week since early August. Markets are also watching rate expectations, with investors weighing the chance of further interest rate rises in the US.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions, savings and investment funds, and tech giants such as Nvidia now carry great weight in the major indexes.

levels.headline: US stocks end Friday mixed: S&P 500 down 0.4% to 7,561.67, Nasdaq down 0.91%, Dow up 0.1%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 finished down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday 13 November, the last completed session. The Nasdaq Composite lost 0.91% to close at 25,136.27, but the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to 52,347.55, CNBC reported.
Nvidia was the main drag on technology shares. It fell again after the departure of its chief executive and founder, Jensen Huang, adding to its losses earlier in the week.
Still, all three main indexes had their strongest week since early August, so the week as a whole was a good one for investors. US markets open again on Monday. Traders are also keeping an eye on whether interest rates may rise further.
levels.why: Moves in the biggest US stocks change the value of many people's pensions and investment funds.

levels.headline: US shares slip on Friday as Nvidia falls, but the week was still a strong one
levels.body:
The S&P 500, an index of 500 big US companies, closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday 13 November. That was the last full trading day before today. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.91% to 25,136.27, while the Dow Jones index, which tracks 30 large firms, rose 0.1% to 52,347.55.
Nvidia, a leading maker of computer chips for artificial intelligence, dragged tech shares lower. Its shares fell again after its chief executive and founder, Jensen Huang, left the company.
Despite the dip, CNBC said all three indexes had their best week since early August. US markets reopen on Monday, and investors are watching for signs of higher interest rates.
levels.why: Share prices feed through to pensions and savings, and affect how confident businesses feel.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends Friday slightly lower, but all three main indexes had their best week since August
levels.body:
The S&P 500, which tracks 500 of the biggest US companies, ended Friday 13 November down 0.4% at 7,561.67. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, fell 0.91% to 25,136.27. The Dow, which follows 30 large companies, edged up 0.1% to 52,347.55.
Nvidia, a company that makes chips used in artificial intelligence, saw its shares drop again after its boss, Jensen Huang, left. Because Nvidia is so big, its moves pull the whole market.
Even so, the week was good overall: all three indexes had their best week since early August. US markets are closed at the weekend and open again on Monday. Investors are also thinking about whether interest rates will go up.
levels.why: Many pension funds hold these shares, so their ups and downs matter to ordinary savers.

levels.headline: US shares fell slightly on Friday, but it was still a good week overall
levels.body:
The S&P 500 is a measure of how 500 of the biggest US companies are doing. On Friday 13 November it fell 0.4% to 7,561.67. The Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, fell 0.91%. The Dow, which follows 30 large companies, rose 0.1%.
Nvidia, a company that makes computer chips used for artificial intelligence, saw its share price fall again after its boss, Jensen Huang, left. Nvidia is so big that when its price moves, the whole market feels it.
Even so, the week was a good one. All three measures had their best week since early August. US markets are closed at weekends and open again on Monday.
levels.why: Many people have savings or pensions linked to shares, so price changes can matter to them.

levels.headline: US stock markets dipped on Friday, though the week was a good one
levels.body:
The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big US companies, and the number that shows how their shares are doing. On Friday 13 November it fell 0.4% to 7,561.67. The Nasdaq, full of tech firms, fell 0.91%. The Dow, which follows 30 large firms, rose a little, by 0.1%.
A big company called Nvidia, which makes computer chips for artificial intelligence, saw its share price fall again. Its boss, Jensen Huang, has left. Because Nvidia is so large, it can pull the whole market down.
Even so, it was the best week for all three since early August. US markets are shut at weekends and open again on Monday.
levels.why: Share prices can change the value of savings and pensions.

levels.headline: US shares went down a little on Friday
levels.body:
A stock market is a place where people buy and sell small pieces of companies, called shares. The S&P 500 shows how 500 big US companies are doing. On Friday 13 November, it went down by 0.4%. That is a small drop.
Another list, the Nasdaq, went down by 0.91%. It has lots of technology companies. A third list, the Dow, went up by 0.1%.
A company called Nvidia makes chips for computers. Its boss left, and people sold its shares, so the price fell. It is a very big company, so it pulled the others down.
Still, it was a good week. All three lists had their best week since early August. The markets open again on Monday.
levels.why: Share prices show how people feel about companies, and they can affect savings.

levels.headline: US share prices fell a little, but the week was good
levels.body:
Some companies sell tiny pieces of themselves. These are called shares. Anyone can buy one. When lots of people want a share, its price goes up. When people sell, it goes down.
On Friday 13 November, the prices of shares in 500 big US companies, as a group, went down 0.4%. That is a small drop. Prices of tech companies went down more. The prices of 30 other big companies went up a tiny bit.
One company, Nvidia, makes computer chips. Its boss left, and its share price fell.
The whole week was still good, with the best prices since early August. The markets are closed on weekends. They open again on Monday.
levels.why: Share prices tell us how people feel about companies, and many families save money in shares.

levels.headline: Share prices wobbled on Friday
levels.body:
Think of a school fair where children swap cards. If everyone wants one card, its price goes up. If nobody wants it, the price goes down. Shares in companies work a bit like that.
On Friday, the prices of shares in lots of big American companies went down by a small amount. The shares in a few companies went up a tiny bit. One big company, Nvidia, makes the chips inside computers. Its boss left, so its price dropped.
But it was still a good week. Prices were the best for months. The market is closed at the weekend and opens again on Monday.
Grown-ups often save money in shares, so they like to watch the prices.
levels.why: Grown-ups save money in shares, so changes in the price matter to many families.

levels.headline: The money market had a small wobble
levels.body:
Have you ever swapped football stickers? Some stickers are very popular, and everybody wants them. Their price goes up. Others are less popular.
Big companies have something like stickers called shares. People buy and sell them. On Friday in America, lots of shares went down a tiny bit, like a sticker losing a little bit of its swap value. A few went up a tiny bit.
One big company, called Nvidia, makes the chips that help computers think. Its boss left and people got worried, so its price fell.
But it was still a good week for most shares. They did better than they had for months. The shops where shares are sold open again on Monday.
levels.why: Many families save money in shares, so it is good to know how they are doing.

headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate by 0.25 points to 4% and warns inflation could near 5% by mid-2027

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences borrowing and saving costs.
The rate at which prices rise over time.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate by 0.25 points to 4% and warns inflation could near 5% by mid-2027
levels.body:
On 5 November the Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4%, its first increase since 2023. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1, with one member wanting a bigger rise of 0.5 points.
The Bank said it expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027, well above its 2% target, and it raised its forecast for 2026 growth to 1.6%. The rise in energy and fuel prices linked to the conflict between the US and Iran is the main risk it cites.
CNBC reported that, according to LSEG data, markets see about a 73% chance of another rise at the December meeting. Higher Bank Rate usually pushes up the cost of mortgages and loans, while it can improve returns for savers.
levels.why: Interest rates shape what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank raises rates to 4%, the first rise since 2023, and expects inflation near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England increased its key interest rate by 0.25 points to 4% on 5 November, the first rise since 2023. Eight members of its Monetary Policy Committee voted for the rise and one wanted a larger 0.5 point increase.
The Bank now expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027, far above its 2% target. It raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.6%. Higher energy and fuel costs linked to the US-Iran conflict are the main concern.
Markets expect further action. Data from LSEG, cited by CNBC, suggested roughly a 73% chance of another increase in December. Borrowers on variable rates could face higher repayments, while savers may see better returns.
levels.why: Higher rates make borrowing dearer for households and firms and can slow the economy.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts interest rates to 4% and warns prices could rise faster
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%, the first rise since 2023. On 5 November, eight of nine members of its rate-setting committee backed the move, while one wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank says inflation, the speed at which prices rise, could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. Its target is 2%. It blames higher energy and fuel prices linked to the conflict between the US and Iran. It also raised its forecast for growth this year to 1.6%.
Markets think another rise in December is likely, at around 73% according to LSEG data. This usually means higher costs for people with mortgages and loans, but better rates for savers.
levels.why: Rates affect mortgage bills, loan costs and the interest paid on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% as it expects inflation to climb
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on 5 November. It is the first rise since 2023. Eight of the nine members voted for the rise, and one wanted a bigger one.
The Bank said it expects inflation, the rate at which prices go up, to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. Its target is 2%. Higher energy and petrol costs linked to the war involving Iran are a main cause. It also raised its forecast for growth this year to 1.6%.
Markets think another increase may follow in December. For people with mortgages or loans, higher rates can mean bigger repayments. Savers may earn more.
levels.why: The decision affects the cost of mortgages and the return on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England put up interest rates to 4%, because it fears prices will keep rising fast
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the UK's central bank. Its job is to keep prices steady. On 5 November it raised its main interest rate to 4%, up a quarter of a point. This is the first rise since 2023.
Prices are rising faster because of dearer energy and petrol, linked to the war involving Iran. The Bank thinks price rises could reach about 5% a year by mid-2027. Its goal is 2%. Raising rates is its main way to slow price rises down.
Most of the Bank's committee agreed, and one wanted a bigger rise. Markets think another rise may come in December. Mortgages and loans may cost more, but savings may earn more.
levels.why: A higher rate can make mortgages cost more, but it can also help savers.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% because prices are rising too fast
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the UK's central bank. On 5 November it raised its main interest rate, called Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%. It is the first rise since 2023. Almost all of the Bank's rate-setting committee agreed, and one person wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank is worried because prices could rise by about 5% a year by the middle of 2027. It wants them to rise by 2%. Energy and petrol cost more because of a conflict involving Iran, and that pushes other prices up.
Higher interest rates make people borrow and spend less, which helps slow price rises. But they also make mortgages and loans cost more. Savers may earn more. Markets think another rise may come in December.
levels.why: A higher rate makes loans dearer but can help savers.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raised interest rates because prices are going up too fast
levels.body:
The Bank of England is in charge of keeping prices steady in the UK. It sets a rate of interest. This is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get paid when you save. On 5 November, it raised that rate to 4%. It was 3.75% before.
The Bank did this because prices are going up fast. Fuel and energy cost more, because of a war involving Iran. The Bank thinks prices could be going up by about 5% a year by mid-2027. It wants that to be 2%.
A higher rate can slow down price rises. But it can make mortgages and loans cost more. Savers may get more. More rises may come in December.
levels.why: Interest rates change how much families pay for loans and earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England made borrowing a bit more expensive
levels.body:
The Bank of England looks after the money of the whole country. It can decide how much it costs to borrow money. This is called the interest rate. If you borrow money, you pay a bit extra. If you save money, you get a bit extra.
On 5 November, the Bank raised the rate a little, to 4. Prices have been going up fast. Things like petrol and gas cost more. The Bank wants prices to stop rising so quickly.
When borrowing costs more, people spend less. That can slow price rises down. But it also means families with a mortgage may pay more each month. People who save may get a little more.
levels.why: It changes how much families pay when they borrow and earn when they save.

levels.headline: The Bank of England changed the cost of borrowing
levels.body:
Imagine you lend your friend some pocket money. You might ask for a little extra back, as a thank you. That extra is like interest.
The Bank of England is like the big bank for the whole country. It decides how much extra people must pay when they borrow. On 5 November it said the extra should go up a little.
This is because sweets, food and petrol are all costing more. When money is dearer to borrow, people buy a bit less, and prices may stop climbing so fast.
But it can be hard for families who borrowed money to buy a house. They may have to pay more each month. People with savings may get a little more.
levels.why: It changes how much families pay for loans and how much they earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England said borrowing money will cost a bit more
levels.body:
Do you know how a piggy bank works? You put money in, and it stays safe. Real banks also keep grown-ups' money and lend money out. When they lend, the person who borrows pays back a little extra. That extra is called interest.
The Bank of England is the boss of banks in our country. It can say how big that little extra should be. On 5 November it said it should go up a little.
Why? Because things in shops are costing more, like petrol and food. If the extra is bigger, people spend less, and prices may stop growing.
Some families may have to pay a bit more each month for their homes.
levels.why: It affects how much money families have to pay back and how much they can save.

headline: UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, with services and AI-related demand cited as drivers

terms.meaning: The total value of goods and services produced in a country, used to measure the size of the economy.
A three-month period used to report economic figures.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, with services and AI-related demand cited as drivers
levels.body:
The UK economy grew 0.7% in the July to September quarter, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Output was 1.9% higher than a year earlier. In September alone, GDP rose 0.2% after no growth in August.
Services drove the gain, and reports said demand linked to artificial intelligence was an extra engine of growth. Euronews and CNBC both reported the figures.
The figures arrived a week after the Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4%. The Bank has raised its forecast for 2026 growth to 1.6%, but analysts cited in the reports expect growth to slow in late 2026 and into 2027. A key risk is the effect of the US-Iran conflict on energy prices. GDP, or gross domestic product, is the main measure of the size of the economy.
levels.why: Economic growth affects jobs, wages and how much the government can raise in tax.

levels.headline: UK GDP rose 0.7% in July to September, helped by services and AI demand
levels.body:
The ONS reports that UK gross domestic product grew 0.7% in the third quarter of 2026. Output was 1.9% higher than a year earlier, and monthly GDP rose 0.2% in September after being flat in August.
Services led the growth. Reports also pointed to demand linked to artificial intelligence as an additional boost.
The figures come soon after the Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% and lifted its 2026 growth forecast to 1.6%. Analysts, however, expect the pace to ease in late 2026 and into 2027. Energy prices, affected by the conflict between the US and Iran, are seen as the main risk.
levels.why: Growth helps jobs and wages, but slower growth could mean tighter public finances.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.7% between July and September, official figures show
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the three months from July to September, the Office for National Statistics said. That is 1.9% bigger than a year earlier. In September alone the economy grew 0.2%, after no growth in August.
Most of the growth came from services, such as shops, hotels and finance. Reports said demand linked to artificial intelligence gave an extra boost.
The Bank of England recently raised interest rates and expects 1.6% growth this year. But analysts think growth will slow at the end of 2026 and into 2027. Higher energy prices because of the war involving Iran are a main risk.
levels.why: A growing economy usually means more jobs and more money for public services.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% in the third quarter, led by services
levels.body:
Britain's economy grew by 0.7% in the three months from July to September, the Office for National Statistics reported. That means the country produced 1.9% more than a year earlier. In September, it grew 0.2% after no growth in August.
Services, the part of the economy that includes shops, restaurants and banks, led the growth. Some reports said business demand linked to artificial intelligence helped too.
The Bank of England thinks the economy will grow 1.6% this year, but experts think growth will slow as 2026 ends. The biggest worry is energy prices, which are higher because of the conflict involving Iran and the US.
levels.why: Growth affects jobs, pay and how much tax the government collects.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew by 0.7% over the summer and autumn months
levels.body:
The UK economy is the total of everything we make and sell. Official statisticians measure it every three months. For July to September it grew by 0.7%. That is a good rise. It is also 1.9% bigger than a year ago.
Most of the growth came from services. These are jobs where people do things for others, such as in shops, hotels and offices. Some reports said companies buying artificial intelligence services also helped.
The Bank of England expects growth of 1.6% this year. But experts think growth will slow soon. The worry is that energy costs are going up because of a war involving Iran.
levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and pay, but slower growth could hurt.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September, mostly thanks to services
levels.body:
The economy is everything that people in the UK make and sell. Official statisticians count it every three months. For July to September, it grew by 0.7%. That is 1.9% bigger than a year ago. In September alone it grew by 0.2%.
Most of the growth came from services. These are jobs where people do things for others, such as working in shops, hotels or banks. Some reports said business demand for artificial intelligence helped too.
The Bank of England expects growth of 1.6% this year. But experts think growth will slow at the end of 2026, because energy costs more after the conflict involving Iran and the US. Higher costs leave families and firms with less to spend.
levels.why: A growing economy usually means more jobs and more money for public services.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September
levels.body:
The economy means all the things people in the UK make and sell. The experts who count it said it grew by 0.7% in the three months from July to September. That is a good amount. It is also bigger than a year ago.
Most of the growth came from services. Those are jobs like working in shops, hotels or banks. Some computer firms made more money too, as businesses bought new artificial intelligence tools.
But some experts think growth will slow soon. One worry is that energy now costs more, because of a war in the Middle East. When energy costs more, businesses and families have less to spend on other things.
levels.why: When the economy grows, there are usually more jobs and more money to spend.

levels.headline: The UK made and sold more things this autumn
levels.body:
The economy is all the things people make and sell in a country. Every three months, experts count it up. This time it showed that the UK made and sold 0.7% more than the three months before. That is a good sign.
Most of the extra came from jobs where people help others. This includes shopkeepers, hotel workers and people in banks. Computer helpers called artificial intelligence also helped.
But experts think growth may slow soon. Gas and petrol cost more because of a war far away. When these cost more, people have less money left to spend. So growth might slow down next year.
levels.why: A bigger economy can mean more jobs and more money for hospitals and schools.

levels.headline: The UK had a good three months of making and selling
levels.body:
Think of a class bake sale. If this term the class sells more cakes than last term, then the sale did well. The country has a big sale like that too. It is called the economy.
Experts count up how much the whole country makes and sells. For the last few months it went up by 0.7%. That is a good rise. Shops, hotels and offices all helped.
But some experts think the next few months may be slower. Things like petrol and gas now cost more, because of a war far away. If you have to pay more for those, you have less to spend on cakes!
levels.why: When the country does well, there are often more jobs and more money for things like schools.

levels.headline: The country sold a few more cakes
levels.body:
Imagine your whole town has a big market. Many people sell things there. Some sell cakes, some sell toys and some help with computers.
Experts counted how many things the whole town sold in the last three months. They found it was a bit more than before. This is called growth. It is a good thing, because it can mean more jobs and money.
But the experts also think the market may get a bit quieter soon. Some things, like petrol, now cost more. That is because of a war in a faraway place. When things cost more, people have less left to buy cakes and toys.
We will see what happens next.
levels.why: When more is made and sold, more grown-ups can have jobs.

headline: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September; October's figure is due on 18 November

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of inflation.
The rate at which prices rise over time.

levels.headline: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September; October's figure is due on 18 November
levels.body:
Annual UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August, according to the latest figures cited by Trading Economics. Higher energy and motor fuel prices were the main drivers.
The next figure, for October, is due on Wednesday 18 November. It will be closely watched because the Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November and says it expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027. The Bank's target is 2%.
Markets were pricing a roughly 73% chance of a further rise in December, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC. Inflation measures how fast prices rise: at 3.5%, something that cost £100 a year ago would now typically cost £103.50.
levels.why: Inflation determines how far wages, benefits and savings go in the shops.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbed to 3.5% in September from 3.1%, driven by energy and fuel
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the year to September, from 3.1% in August. Trading Economics reports that higher energy and motor fuel prices were the main factors.
The October reading is due on 18 November. Economists will look at it closely because the Bank of England lifted Bank Rate to 4% earlier this month and expects inflation to reach about 5% by mid-2027, compared with its 2% target.
CNBC reported that markets saw about a 73% chance of another rate rise in December. At 3.5%, goods that cost £100 a year earlier would typically cost around £103.50 now.
levels.why: Rising prices reduce what wages and savings can buy and influence interest rate decisions.

levels.headline: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, with energy and fuel the main causes
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK went up to 3.5% in the year to September. It had been 3.1% in August. That means prices, on average, were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. Higher energy and petrol costs were the main reason.
The next figure, for October, will be published on 18 November. Many people will watch it, because the Bank of England put up interest rates to 4% earlier this month. It says inflation could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. Its target is 2%.
Markets think a further rate rise in December is quite likely. An item that cost £100 last year would usually cost about £103.50 now.
levels.why: It affects the cost of living and how interest rates change.

levels.headline: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September as energy and petrol cost more
levels.body:
Inflation is the speed at which prices rise. In the year to September, it rose to 3.5% in the UK, up from 3.1% in August. That means something that cost £100 a year ago would usually cost around £103.50 now.
The main causes were dearer energy and petrol. Much of this is linked to the conflict involving the US and Iran.
The figure for October will come out on 18 November. People will watch it closely. The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% earlier this month and expects inflation to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. Its aim is 2%. Markets think another rise in rates could come in December.
levels.why: If prices rise faster than pay, people can afford less.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK rose faster in September, by 3.5% over the year
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices go up. In September, prices in the UK were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. In August, the figure was 3.1%. So prices are rising faster. Something that cost £100 last year costs about £103.50 now.
The main causes were higher energy and petrol costs. These are linked to a war involving Iran and the US.
The next figure will be out on 18 November. The Bank of England wants inflation to be 2%. It thinks inflation could rise to about 5% by the middle of next year. It has put up interest rates to try to slow prices down.
levels.why: When prices rise faster than pay, families can buy less with their money.

levels.headline: UK prices rose 3.5% over the year to September, faster than in August
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices go up. In the year to September, prices in the UK rose by 3.5% on average. In August, the figure was 3.1%. So an item that cost £100 a year ago now costs around £103.50.
The main causes were higher energy and petrol prices, linked to a conflict involving Iran and the US. Petrol and energy are used to make and move many other things, so their cost spreads through the shops.
The next figure, for October, will be out on 18 November. The Bank of England wants inflation to be 2% but thinks it could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. That is why it has raised interest rates, to try to slow prices down.
levels.why: If prices rise faster than pay, people can buy less with their money.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are rising faster
levels.body:
Inflation means that prices go up over time. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. That is faster than in August, when it was 3.1%. So something that cost £100 a year ago now costs about £103.50.
The main reasons were that energy and petrol cost more. This is because of a war involving Iran.
The next number will come out on 18 November. The Bank of England wants prices to rise by only 2% a year. It thinks they may rise by around 5% by next summer. That is why it raised interest rates. Higher rates can slow price rises down, but they can also make loans cost more.
levels.why: When prices go up faster than pay, people can afford less.

levels.headline: Things in shops cost more than last year
levels.body:
Inflation is a big word. It means prices going up. If a toy cost £10 last year and costs £10.35 now, that is a rise of 3.5%. That is what has happened to prices in the UK on average.
In August prices were going up a bit more slowly. Now it is a bit faster. The main reason is that energy and petrol cost more. That is because of a war far away.
The next count will be on 18 November. The Bank of England wants prices to go up by only 2%. It thinks they may go up by 5% next summer. So it has made it dearer to borrow money.
levels.why: When prices rise faster than pay, families can buy less.

levels.headline: Prices are creeping up
levels.body:
Imagine a packet of sweets cost £1 last year. This year it costs a little more. That is called inflation. It means that the price of things goes up.
In the UK, prices are now a bit higher than last year. If you had £100 to spend last year, you would now need about £103.50 to buy the same things.
Petrol and gas cost more, so lots of other things cost more too. That is because a war far away has made them dearer.
Another count of prices will be made on 18 November. The Bank of England is a big bank. It wants prices to go up slowly, not quickly.
levels.why: If prices go up a lot, a family's pocket money or wages do not buy as much.

levels.headline: Things cost a little more than they used to
levels.body:
When you go to the shop with your pocket money, you might notice that sweets cost more than last year. This is called inflation. It means prices are growing.
A grown-up count says that, on average, things in the UK cost 3.5% more than a year ago. That is a small bit more. If your pocket money stays the same, you can buy a little less.
Grown-ups think this is because petrol and gas cost more, and those are used to make and move lots of things.
They will count again on 18 November. A big bank wants prices to go up only a very little.
levels.why: If things cost more and pocket money or wages stay the same, you can buy less.

headline: Healey's first Budget raises the bank surcharge to 6%, rules out tax rises on wages and dividends, and extends an energy bill tax cut

terms.meaning: The government's yearly statement on taxes and spending.
An extra tax added on top of an existing tax.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget raises the bank surcharge to 6%, rules out tax rises on wages and dividends, and extends an energy bill tax cut
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October. The main revenue raiser was a temporary 3 percentage point rise in the bank surcharge, taking it to 6%. It is due to start in January and end 15 months later. Gambling businesses and vape shops were also targeted with new taxes.
Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. A tax cut on household electricity was extended, and a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was dropped. A First-Time Buyer ISA is to replace the Lifetime ISA, and low-income pensioners are set to pay less tax or none.
Business Asset Disposal Relief's threshold falls from £1m to £500,000, while a new Founder's Relief applies a 10% rate on lifetime gains up to £10m. Before the Budget, John Healey faced a test from bond markets.
levels.why: The Budget sets the taxes people and businesses pay and affects bills, savings and house buying.

levels.headline: Budget 2026: bank tax up, no rise on wages or dividends, First-Time Buyer ISA to replace Lifetime ISA
levels.body:
John Healey presented his first Budget as Chancellor on 28 October. Banks will pay a bank surcharge raised by 3 points to 6%, temporary, from January for 15 months. Gambling and vape businesses face new taxes.
He pledged no tax rises on wages or dividends, extended a household electricity tax cut and cancelled a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds. A First-Time Buyer ISA will replace the Lifetime ISA, and low-income pensioners should pay less tax or none.
Business Asset Disposal Relief's threshold falls from £1m to £500,000, but a new Founder's Relief taxes lifetime gains up to £10m at 10%. Coverage noted that the Chancellor faced scrutiny from bond markets beforehand.
levels.why: The measures change what banks, firms, savers and first-time buyers pay or keep.

levels.headline: Chancellor's first Budget taxes banks more and avoids new taxes on wages
levels.body:
John Healey gave his first Budget as Chancellor on 28 October. The biggest money-raiser was a higher tax on banks. The bank surcharge goes up by 3 points to 6%. It is meant to be temporary, starting in January and lasting 15 months. Gambling firms and vape shops will also pay more.
He said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. A tax cut on household electricity was extended, and a planned cut to the amount people can hold in tax-free savings was dropped. A First-Time Buyer ISA will replace the Lifetime ISA.
Low-income pensioners will pay less tax or none. Owners selling businesses will see a lower limit on a tax break, but founders get a new relief.
levels.why: It shapes tax bills, energy costs and help for savers and first-time buyers.

levels.headline: Budget: banks to pay more tax, but no rise in tax on wages or dividends
levels.body:
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, set out his first Budget. This is the government's yearly plan for tax and spending. The biggest rise was an extra tax on banks. The bank surcharge goes up from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January. Betting firms and vape shops will pay new taxes too.
Mr Healey promised no tax rises on wages or dividends. A tax cut on household electricity will carry on, and a plan to cut tax-free savings limits was dropped. A First-Time Buyer ISA will replace the Lifetime ISA, a savings account for buying a first home.
Low-income pensioners should pay less tax or none. Rules on a tax break for selling a business were changed, too.
levels.why: It affects bills, savings and taxes for many households and businesses.

levels.headline: The Chancellor's Budget put more tax on banks but not on people's pay
levels.body:
A Budget is a yearly plan about money. The government says how much tax it will collect and how it will spend it. On 28 October, the Chancellor, John Healey, gave his first one.
Banks will pay more tax. An extra tax on their profits will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months, starting in January. Gambling and vape shops will also pay new taxes.
He said that wages and company dividends, which are payments to shareholders, will not face higher tax. Electricity will keep a tax cut. A new savings account for first-time home buyers will replace an older one. Some poorer pensioners will pay less tax or none.
levels.why: The plan decides who pays tax and what help people get.

levels.headline: The Chancellor's Budget puts more tax on banks but not on wages
levels.body:
A Budget is the government's yearly plan for tax and spending. On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, set out his first. The main extra tax falls on banks. Their surcharge, an extra tax on profits, rises from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January. Gambling and vape businesses will also pay new taxes.
Mr Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends, which are payments to people who own shares. A tax cut on household electricity will carry on. A planned cut to tax-free savings limits was dropped.
A First-Time Buyer ISA, a tax-free savings account for a first home, will replace the Lifetime ISA. Low-income pensioners should pay less tax or none.
levels.why: It decides who pays tax and what help people get.

levels.headline: The government said banks must pay more tax
levels.body:
Every year, the government makes a big plan about money. It is called the Budget. It says what tax people and firms must pay. On 28 October, a new Chancellor, John Healey, gave his first plan.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits. The extra will go up to 6%, for a bit over a year, starting in January. Betting shops and vape shops will pay new taxes too.
He said people who work will not pay more tax on their pay. Electricity bills will stay a little lower because of a tax cut. People who want to buy their first home will get a new kind of savings account. Some older people with low income will pay less tax.
levels.why: It decides what tax people pay and what help they get with bills and homes.

levels.headline: The government planned how it will use money
levels.body:
The government needs money to pay for things like schools, hospitals and roads. It gets that money from tax. A Budget is a plan for what tax to collect.
On 28 October, a person called the Chancellor, John Healey, shared a new plan. He said banks will pay more tax for a little over a year. Shops that sell gambling and vapes will pay more too.
He said people who work will not pay more tax on their pay. People who are saving to buy their first home will get a special savings account. Some older people with small incomes will pay less tax. Electricity will stay a bit cheaper, because a tax on it was cut.
levels.why: Taxes pay for things like schools and hospitals, so the plan matters to everyone.

levels.headline: The government made a plan for its money
levels.body:
Imagine that a class has a money jar. Everyone puts in a little bit. The class uses the jar to buy paper, pens and games. The government has a jar like this too, but it is huge. The money in it comes from tax.
On 28 October, a person called the Chancellor, John Healey, shared a new plan. He said banks must put in more money for a while. He did not ask workers to put in more.
He also said that there will be a new savings jar for people saving up to buy their first home. And some older people with little money will pay less.
levels.why: Taxes pay for schools, hospitals and roads that we all use.

levels.headline: The Chancellor made a plan for the nation's money jar
levels.body:
Do you remember how your school has a money jar for the class fun day? Everyone puts in a little bit. Then the class uses the money for nice things.
A whole country has a money jar like that too. It is much bigger! Grown-ups put money into it by paying taxes. It pays for hospitals, schools and roads.
Once a year, a person called the Chancellor makes a plan for the jar. This year, the Chancellor is called John Healey. He said banks should put in more for a little while. He said people who go to work should not need to put in more.
He also helped people saving for a first home, and older people with little money.
levels.why: Taxes pay for things we all use, like schools, hospitals and roads.

headline: Anthropic's updated IPO filing proposes 825 million shares at $70 to $78, valuing the AI firm at up to $1.4 trillion, with pricing planned for 18 November

terms.meaning: Initial public offering: the first time a company sells shares to the public on a stock market.
An estimate of how much a company is worth in total.

levels.headline: Anthropic's updated IPO filing proposes 825 million shares at $70 to $78, valuing the AI firm at up to $1.4 trillion, with pricing planned for 18 November
levels.body:
Anthropic's updated filing for its stock market flotation proposes selling 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each, according to CNBC. At the top of that range the offer would raise $64.35 billion and value the company at up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, which counts options and other share awards. On a basic count, that top price implies about $1 trillion.
The company plans to price its shares on 18 November and begin trading the following day, though another CNBC report gave 19 November for the listing, so timing may still shift.
The valuation is below the $2 trillion that was reported in October, and above the $965 billion at which Anthropic raised money in May. Analysts are divided: one called it the most ridiculous IPO of the year, while CNBC's Jim Cramer argued its revenue growth helps justify a trillion-dollar-plus value.
levels.why: The listing is a major test of how much investors are willing to pay for artificial intelligence companies.

levels.headline: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 a share, valuing it at up to $1.4 trillion
levels.body:
Anthropic has updated its IPO filing to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each. At the top price, the sale would raise $64.35 billion and value the company at up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, or about $1 trillion on a basic count, CNBC reports.
The company plans to set the price on 18 November and start trading the next day. Another CNBC piece suggested 19 November for the listing, so dates may move.
Investors had earlier talked of a $2 trillion valuation, so this is lower, but it is above the $965 billion valuation from a May funding round. Critics doubt the price, while supporters point to rapid revenue growth.
levels.why: A very large listing can affect markets and tests investors' appetite for AI firms.

levels.headline: AI company Anthropic is set to go public, valued at up to $1.4 trillion
levels.body:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI assistant, has said it will sell 825 million shares to the public at $70 to $78 each. At the top price, that would raise about $64 billion and value the firm at up to $1.4 trillion once options and similar awards are counted. Without them, the figure is about $1 trillion.
It plans to set the final price on 18 November and start trading the day after, although one report gave 19 November.
The value is lower than the $2 trillion mentioned in October. Some analysts think the price is too high, while others say strong revenue growth supports it.
levels.why: It shows how much investors think AI companies are worth, and how risky that may be.

levels.headline: Anthropic plans to start selling shares to the public next week, valuing itself at around $1 trillion or more
levels.body:
Anthropic, which makes the Claude AI assistant, plans to sell shares to the public for the first time. This is called an IPO. It wants to sell 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 each. At the top price it would raise about $64 billion.
That would value the company at about $1 trillion, or $1.4 trillion if you include share awards for staff and others. It plans to set the price on 18 November, and trading should start the next day.
Some analysts think this is too high, and one called it the most ridiculous IPO of the year. Others say fast-growing sales justify the price. Earlier talk of a $2 trillion value has cooled.
levels.why: People who invest or save through pension funds may end up holding such shares.

levels.headline: Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, is about to sell its shares to the public
levels.body:
Anthropic is a company that makes an AI helper called Claude. Until now only a small number of investors owned shares in it. Now it wants to sell shares to anyone through the stock market. This is called an IPO.
It wants to sell 825 million shares for $70 to $78 each. That could raise around $64 billion. The shares would make the whole company worth about $1 trillion, or $1.4 trillion if you count extra shares promised to staff and others. It plans to set the price on 18 November.
Some experts think the price is far too high. Others say the company is growing so fast that it is worth it.
levels.why: Big share sales can change how people feel about technology companies and their investments.

levels.headline: Anthropic is selling shares to the public for the first time, with pricing planned for 18 November
levels.body:
Anthropic is the company that makes the Claude AI assistant. Until now it has been owned by a limited group of investors. Now it plans to sell shares on the stock market, which is called an IPO, short for initial public offering.
It wants to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each, which could raise about $64 billion. That would make the company worth about $1 trillion, or $1.4 trillion if share awards for staff and others are counted. The price is due to be set on 18 November, with trading starting the next day.
Some analysts think the price is far too high. Others say the company's sales are growing quickly enough to justify it. Earlier talk of a $2 trillion value has cooled.
levels.why: If a share is priced too high, buyers can lose money when it falls.

levels.headline: Anthropic is going to let the public buy its shares
levels.body:
Anthropic makes an AI helper called Claude. It plans to sell shares to the public for the first time. A share is a small piece of a company. This kind of sale is called an IPO.
It wants to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each. That would bring in about $64 billion, a huge amount. It would make the whole company worth at least $1 trillion. That is why people are talking about it so much.
The price will be set on 18 November, and trading should start the next day. Some experts say the company is not worth that much. Others think it grows so fast that the price is fair.
levels.why: If a share price is too high, buyers can lose money when it falls.

levels.headline: A big computer company wants to sell shares to the public
levels.body:
A company called Anthropic makes an AI helper called Claude. It wants to let everyone buy a small piece of it. These small pieces are called shares.
It will sell lots of shares, and each costs between $70 and $78. If all are sold, the company will get about $64 billion. That is a very big pile of money. The shares make the whole company worth about $1 trillion. That is a number with twelve zeros!
The price will be set on 18 November. People will be able to buy shares the next day. Some experts say the price is too high. Others think the company will grow so much that it is worth it.
levels.why: If lots of people buy shares at a price that is too high, they can lose money.

levels.headline: A company wants to sell tiny pieces of itself
levels.body:
Imagine you make friendship bracelets and they are very popular. You might say to friends, I will sell you a tiny piece of my bracelet business. If the business does well, your piece is worth more.
A company called Anthropic is doing something like this, but it is huge. It makes a computer helper called Claude. It wants to sell lots of tiny pieces, called shares, to anyone. Each piece costs about $70 to $78.
Some people think the company is worth a gigantic amount. Others think the price is too big, like paying a lot for one friendship bracelet. We will find out soon, because the sale is on 18 November.
levels.why: If you pay too much for something, it can lose value later.

levels.headline: A company is asking people to buy a tiny bit of it
levels.body:
Do you ever collect stickers? Imagine one rare sticker costs lots of money because everyone wants it. But what if you pay so much and then nobody else wants it? Then your sticker is worth less.
A company called Anthropic makes a computer helper called Claude. It is going to sell tiny bits of itself, called shares, to people. Lots of grown-ups want them, because the company is growing fast.
But some people think the price is too high, like paying a huge amount for a sticker. Others think the company will do really well. We will find out after the sale on 18 November.
levels.why: Grown-ups want to be careful with money, so they think hard about prices.

headline: Eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, a three-year high, as energy prices surged and an ECB rate rise looms

terms.meaning: The group of EU countries that use the euro as their currency.
The interest rate the ECB pays banks that park money with it.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, a three-year high, as energy prices surged and an ECB rate rise looms
levels.body:
Eurostat's flash estimate put euro area inflation at 4% in October, up from 3.8% in September and the highest in three years. Officials said energy costs were the main cause: energy inflation rose to 20.8% from 18.9%. Core inflation, which strips out energy and food, held at 2.5%. The final October reading is due on 18 November.
The European Central Bank kept its deposit facility rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after raising it in June and September. Prediction markets put about an 84% chance on a quarter-point rise at its meeting on 16 and 17 December. A French bond market selloff was cited as a complication.
The rise echoes the UK, where the Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November.
levels.why: Higher prices and likely higher rates affect Europeans' bills and borrowing, and the UK's trade partners.

levels.headline: Euro area inflation reaches 4%, the highest in three years, led by energy costs
levels.body:
Inflation in the euro area rose to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, a three-year high, according to Eurostat's flash estimate. Energy inflation climbed to 20.8% from 18.9%, while core inflation was unchanged at 2.5%.
The final figure is due on 18 November.
The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October after rises in June and September. Prediction markets see about an 84% chance of a quarter-point increase at the 16 and 17 December meeting. A selloff in French government bonds is seen as a complication for the bank.
levels.why: The ECB's decisions influence borrowing costs across the euro area and the value of the euro.

levels.headline: Prices in the eurozone are rising at 4%, the fastest in three years
levels.body:
Prices across the countries that use the euro rose 4% in the year to October, up from 3.8% in September. It is the fastest rate in three years, according to Eurostat's early estimate. Higher energy costs were the main reason. Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year earlier.
Core inflation, which leaves out items like energy and food that can jump around, held steady at 2.5%.
The European Central Bank held its key rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after raising it twice earlier this year. Markets think another quarter-point rise is likely when it meets on 16 and 17 December. A selloff in French government bonds is also a worry.
levels.why: Rising prices and rates affect millions of households and businesses across Europe.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation hits 4%, a three-year high, as energy costs jump
levels.body:
Inflation in the countries that share the euro rose to 4% in October, up from 3.8% a month earlier. That is the highest for three years. The EU's statistics office says energy prices were the main cause. They were 20.8% higher than a year ago.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the euro area, kept its main rate at 2.5% in October. It raised it earlier this year, in June and September.
Traders now think the bank will raise the rate by a quarter of a point at its next meeting, on 16 and 17 December. A big sell-off in French government debt is also on the bank's mind.
levels.why: It means higher bills for people in Europe and may lead to higher borrowing costs.

levels.headline: Prices in countries that use the euro are going up faster
levels.body:
The euro is the money used by many European countries, like France and Germany. Experts say prices in those countries went up 4% over the year to October. That is the fastest in three years. In September it was 3.8%.
The main reason is that energy costs a lot more. It costs about 20.8% more than a year ago. When energy costs more, many other things cost more too.
The bank that looks after the euro is called the European Central Bank. It keeps its main interest rate at 2.5%. People expect it to raise the rate in December, to try to slow price rises. The final October figure will come out on 18 November.
levels.why: When prices rise fast, families in Europe can afford less.

levels.headline: Prices in the euro countries rose 4% in the year to October, the fastest rise in three years
levels.body:
The euro is the money used by many European countries, such as France and Germany. Experts say prices in those countries were 4% higher in October than a year earlier. In September the figure was 3.8%. It is the fastest rise in three years.
The main cause is energy, which cost about 21% more than a year ago. When energy is dear, it costs more to make and move goods, so shop prices rise too.
The European Central Bank looks after the euro and sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It is 2.5% now, and many people expect a rise in December to try to slow prices down. The final October figure comes out on 18 November.
levels.why: Rising prices and dearer loans leave families with less to spend.

levels.headline: Prices in Europe are rising faster, mostly because energy costs more
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe, like France and Germany, use the euro as their money. Prices in these countries are going up. In October they were 4% higher than a year before. That is the fastest in three years.
The main cause is energy. It costs about a fifth more than last year. That makes it dearer to make and move things, so many other items cost more too.
A bank called the European Central Bank looks after the euro. It chooses the interest rate. This is the price of borrowing money. It is 2.5% now. Many people think it will go up in December to try to slow price rises down.
levels.why: Higher prices and dearer loans make life harder for families.

levels.headline: Prices are going up in Europe
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe share the same kind of money. It is called the euro. In those countries, prices are going up faster. In October, things cost 4% more than a year earlier. That is the biggest rise in three years.
The biggest reason is that energy, like gas and electricity, costs a lot more. When energy is dear, shops and factories pay more, so they put up prices.
A big bank looks after the euro. It can make borrowing more expensive to slow prices down. People think it may do that in December. Families who borrow money may then pay more.
levels.why: It means families in Europe may pay more for food, gas and electricity.

levels.headline: Things cost more in Europe
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use a type of money called the euro. It is a bit like the pound, but it belongs to lots of countries.
In those countries, things now cost more than they did last year. Imagine a toy that cost £10 last year, and now costs £10.40. That is what a 4% rise looks like.
The main reason is that energy, like gas and electricity, costs a lot more. Shops and factories need energy, so they put up their prices.
A big bank looks after the euro. It might make borrowing cost more to slow things down. That might happen in December.
levels.why: Higher prices mean people can buy fewer things with the same money.

levels.headline: Prices are rising in countries across the sea
levels.body:
Across the sea from the UK, many countries use money called the euro. The shops there are charging more than before. Last year a sweet might have cost 100 coins. Now it might cost 104 coins.
The reason is that things like gas and electricity cost more. Shops and factories need those things to make and sell sweets and toys. So they must charge more.
A big bank looks after the euro. It might make borrowing money cost more. That can help stop prices from rising so fast. People think it will happen in December.
levels.why: When prices go up, it is harder for families to buy the things they need.

headline: Trump says US has 'won' Iran war as Rubio reports no progress in talks, while ships are still being hit in the Gulf

terms.meaning: Using warships to stop ships entering or leaving a country's ports.
A narrow sea route in the Gulf through which much of the world's oil passes.

levels.headline: Trump says US has 'won' Iran war as Rubio reports no progress in talks, while ships are still being hit in the Gulf
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump said the United States had won the war with Iran and that it was now a matter of closing it out, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio reported no progress in talks, Euronews reported on 9 November. Trump said restarting the war was highly unlikely but left open further strikes if he thought them necessary, tying that to Iran signing a very strong agreement.
Iran says several conditions must be met before nuclear talks: an end to the US naval blockade of its ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, compensation for war damage and an end to hostilities across the region.
The US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz and said it disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman, while Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers hit mines. The latest reports found run to about 9 November.
levels.why: The conflict affects oil prices, inflation and interest rates well beyond the Middle East.

levels.headline: Trump says US has won Iran war, but Rubio reports no progress and shipping attacks continue
levels.body:
President Trump said the US had won the war with Iran, while Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State, reported no progress in talks. Trump called a restart of the war highly unlikely but said he could strike again if Iran did not sign a very strong agreement. The reports are from around 9 November.
Iran says it will not hold nuclear talks until the US ends its naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifts sanctions, unfreezes assets, pays compensation for war damage and ends hostilities across the region.
Meanwhile the US struck Qeshm Island and a vessel in the Gulf of Oman, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
levels.why: Fighting around the Strait of Hormuz can push up oil prices worldwide.

levels.headline: US and Iran are still far apart, with attacks on ships continuing in the Gulf
levels.body:
President Donald Trump says the US has won the war with Iran. But the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, says there has been no progress in talks. Trump says starting the war again is highly unlikely, but he says he could order more strikes if Iran does not sign a very strong deal. These reports date from around 9 November.
Iran says it will not discuss its nuclear programme until the US ends its blockade of Iranian ports, lifts sanctions, releases frozen money, pays for war damage and ends the fighting across the region.
Ships are still being hit. The US struck Qeshm Island and a vessel in the Gulf of Oman, and two tankers hit mines.
levels.why: The Strait of Hormuz carries much of the world's oil, so trouble there affects prices everywhere.

levels.headline: Trump says the US has won the war with Iran, but talks have made no progress
levels.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that the US won the war with Iran. But the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, said there was no progress in talks. Trump said it was highly unlikely that the war would start again, but he said he could still order strikes. These reports are from around 9 November.
Iran says it will not talk about its nuclear programme until several demands are met. These include the end of a US naval blockade, in which warships stop ships from reaching Iranian ports, the lifting of sanctions and payment for war damage.
Ships are still being hit in the Gulf, and the US has struck Qeshm Island.
levels.why: Oil moves through this area, so the conflict affects petrol prices and the cost of living.

levels.headline: The US and Iran are not agreeing, and ships are still being hit
levels.body:
The US and Iran have been in a war. US President Donald Trump now says the US has won. But his Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, says talks to end the dispute have made no progress. These reports are from around 9 November.
Iran says it will not talk about its nuclear plans until the US stops blocking its ports with warships. It also wants sanctions, which are punishments on trade, lifted. And it wants money back that is frozen, and payment for war damage.
Meanwhile ships are still being hit in the Gulf. The US struck an island and a vessel, and two tankers hit mines. Trump says restarting the war is unlikely, but he may still strike.
levels.why: A lot of the world's oil travels through this area, so trouble there can push up prices.

levels.headline: The US and Iran have not agreed on how to end their war, and ships are still being hit
levels.body:
The US and Iran have been in a war. US President Donald Trump says the US has won. But Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, says talks have made no progress. These reports date from around 9 November.
Iran says it will not talk about its nuclear plans until the US ends its naval blockade, which means warships stopping ships from reaching Iranian ports. It also wants sanctions lifted, its frozen money returned and payment for war damage.
Ships are still being hit in the Gulf. The US struck an island called Qeshm and a ship, and two tankers hit mines. Mr Trump says starting the war again is unlikely, but he says he could still strike if Iran does not sign a strong deal.
levels.why: Much of the world's oil moves through this area, so trouble there can raise prices.

levels.headline: The US and Iran still cannot agree on how to end a war
levels.body:
The US and Iran have been in a war. The US President, Donald Trump, says the US has won. His Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, says talks to end it are not getting anywhere. These reports are from around 9 November.
Iran says it will not talk about its nuclear plans until the US stops its ships blocking Iranian ports. It also wants punishments on its trade lifted, its frozen money returned, and payment for war damage.
Ships are still being hit in the Gulf, including by mines. The US says it hit an island and a ship. Mr Trump says starting the war again is unlikely. But he says he could still strike if Iran does not sign a strong deal.
levels.why: The fighting is near the main route for the world's oil, so it can raise petrol prices.

levels.headline: Two countries are still arguing after a war
levels.body:
The US and Iran are two countries that have been at war. The leader of the US, President Trump, says the US has won. But another US leader, Marco Rubio, says that the talks to settle things are not working.
Iran wants some things first. It wants the US to stop its ships blocking Iran's ports. It wants the US to stop punishing Iran's trade. It wants its frozen money back, and money for what was broken in the war.
Ships are still being hit in the sea nearby. Some hit hidden bombs in the water, called mines. The US leader says he does not want the war to start again, but he might still strike.
levels.why: A lot of oil comes through this sea, so fights there can make petrol cost more.

levels.headline: Two countries are still not getting along
levels.body:
Imagine two classes that had a big row in the playground. One class says it won the game. The other class says it does not agree. They try to talk to each other, but it is not going well.
That is a bit like the US and Iran. They had a war, which is much more serious than a playground game. The US leader says the US won. But the talks to make peace are not working.
Iran wants the US to stop blocking its ports first, and give back money it froze. Ships are still getting hurt in the sea nearby. The leaders may need more time to find a way to be friends.
levels.why: When countries argue near an important sea, it can make things more expensive for everyone.

levels.headline: Two countries are still having a big argument
levels.body:
Think of two friends who had a big argument at school. One says, I won. The other says, no way! They try to talk, but nothing seems to change.
That is a bit like what is happening between two countries, the US and Iran. They had a real war, which is much worse than an argument. The leader of the US says his side won. But the countries have not agreed on how to make peace.
Some ships are still being hurt in the sea nearby. The leaders keep talking, but it is hard. Grown-ups hope they will find a way to stop fighting soon.
levels.why: Peace between countries helps people everywhere stay safe and keeps prices steady.

headline: Brent crude near $95 a barrel, down about 13% over the past month on hopes of a US-Iran deal

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
The standard unit for measuring oil, about 159 litres.

levels.headline: Brent crude near $95 a barrel, down about 13% over the past month on hopes of a US-Iran deal
levels.body:
Brent crude was trading near $95 a barrel on 16 November, according to Trading Economics, which showed it at $94.88, down 1.00% on the day. It has fallen 13.39% over the past month, although it is still 47.79% higher than a year ago.
The price has swung with news on the US-Iran conflict. On 2 November, Brent lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 after both sides signalled openness to diplomacy. On 10 November it briefly dipped below $90 for the first time since August and settled at $91.49. On 12 November it settled 3.3% higher at $95.82 after Trump said no Iran deal was needed.
Analysts say oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have largely recovered. ING expects prices to stay sensitive to developments in the Middle East.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and the price of almost everything that is made or moved.

levels.headline: Brent near $95, down on Iran hopes, but still up 48% on a year ago
levels.body:
Brent crude stood near $94.88 a barrel on 16 November, down 1% on the day and down 13.39% over a month, but 47.79% above a year ago, Trading Economics reports.
It has been volatile. It fell 7.6% to $104.77 on 2 November as diplomacy hopes rose, briefly slipped below $90 on 10 November, settling at $91.49, and rose 3.3% to $95.82 on 12 November after comments from Donald Trump.
Analysts say flows through the Strait of Hormuz have largely recovered, easing supply fears. ING expects prices to remain sensitive to Middle East news.
levels.why: Energy prices help drive inflation and so influence interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil prices have fallen back to about $95 a barrel, but are still much higher than a year ago
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main international oil benchmark, was about $94.88 a barrel on 16 November. That is 1% lower than the day before, and 13.39% lower than a month ago. But it is still 47.79% higher than a year ago.
Prices have jumped around with news about the US and Iran. They fell sharply on 2 November when both sides talked about diplomacy, dipped below $90 on 10 November for the first time since August, and rose again on 12 November after comments by President Trump.
