Analysts say oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have mostly recovered. They expect prices to keep reacting to Middle East news.
levels.why: Dearer oil raises petrol and energy bills and can push up prices in shops.

levels.headline: Oil prices drop to around $95 a barrel, but remain far higher than a year ago
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main international price for oil, was about $95 a barrel on 16 November. It is down about 13% over the past month but almost 48% higher than a year ago.
The price has moved sharply on news about the US and Iran. It fell 7.6% on 2 November when both sides seemed open to talks, dipped below $90 briefly on 10 November, and rose on 12 November after President Trump said no deal was needed.
Analysts say shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil route, has largely recovered, which eases supply worries. They say prices will probably stay sensitive to news from the region.
levels.why: Oil prices affect petrol, energy bills and inflation.

levels.headline: The price of oil has come down a bit, but it is still high
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid that is turned into petrol and other fuels. Its price is measured in barrels. One popular price is called Brent. On 16 November it was about $95 a barrel. That is lower than a month ago, when it was about 13% higher. But it is still almost 48% more than a year ago.
The price went up and down a lot because of news about the US and Iran. When it seemed the two countries might talk, the price fell. When there was fighting, it rose.
Experts say oil is moving through the main sea route again. But they say prices may still jump around.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and many other things cost more too.

levels.headline: The price of oil has fallen to about $95 a barrel, but is still far higher than a year ago
levels.body:
Brent is the main international price for oil, which is sold by the barrel. On 16 November it was about $95 a barrel. That is about 13% lower than a month ago, but nearly 48% higher than a year ago.
The price has jumped around because of news about the US and Iran. It fell sharply on 2 November when both sides talked about diplomacy. It dipped below $90 on 10 November, then rose again on 12 November after comments by President Trump.
Experts say ships are mostly getting through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route for oil, so there is less worry about supply. But they say prices may keep reacting to news from the Middle East.
levels.why: Dearer oil can mean higher petrol prices and higher prices in the shops.

levels.headline: Oil costs less than it did last month, but more than a year ago
levels.body:
Oil is dug from the ground and made into petrol and other fuels. It is sold by the barrel. One main price is called Brent. On 16 November it was about $95 a barrel. A month ago it was about 13% higher. A year ago it was a lot lower, almost half the price.
The price goes up and down because of news about a war between the US and Iran. A lot of oil is shipped through a narrow sea called the Strait of Hormuz. When ships there are in danger, the price goes up.
Now more ships are getting through, so the price is lower. But experts say it could change again.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil costs a bit less, but it still costs a lot
levels.body:
Oil comes from under the ground. It is turned into petrol for cars and many other things. Oil is sold by the barrel, which is a big container. On 16 November, one barrel cost about $95.
A month ago it cost more. But a year ago it cost much less. So it is still dear.
The price changes with news. There is a war between the US and Iran. A lot of oil goes by ship through a narrow sea near Iran. If the ships are in danger, the price goes up. Lately more ships have been getting through, so the price has fallen a bit. But it could jump up again.
levels.why: When oil is dear, petrol and lots of other things cost more.

levels.headline: The price of oil has gone down a little
levels.body:
Cars need petrol to go. Petrol is made from oil. Oil is dug out of the ground and sold in big barrels. The price of a barrel goes up and down all the time.
It is now about $95 a barrel. A month ago it was more. It is still much more than last year.
Why does it change? There is a war between two countries far away. Lots of oil goes on ships through a narrow sea near them. If the ships are not safe, the price goes up. Now more ships are getting through. So the price has gone down a little.
When the price of oil is high, trips in a car cost more.
levels.why: When oil costs more, it costs more to move things and for people to travel.

levels.headline: The price of something that makes cars go has dipped
levels.body:
Cars need petrol to go. Petrol comes from oil, which is dug out of the ground. Oil is sold in big barrels, and the price of a barrel goes up and down.
Imagine it is like the price of your favourite sweets. Sometimes the shop makes them cost more. Sometimes it makes them cost less. A month ago, a barrel cost more. Now it costs a little less. But it is still much more than last year.
The price moves when countries have fights, because oil goes across the sea in big ships. If the ships are not safe, the price goes up.
levels.why: When oil costs less, it can help everything get a bit cheaper.

headline: Moscow softens stance on EU role in Ukraine talks as Zelenskyy says US floated Donbas for NATO membership

terms.meaning: An industrial region in eastern Ukraine, partly held by Russia.
A military alliance of mostly European and North American countries.

levels.headline: Moscow softens stance on EU role in Ukraine talks as Zelenskyy says US floated Donbas for NATO membership
levels.body:
Russia has softened its stance on who may take part in Ukraine peace talks, saying it will not dictate whether EU delegates take part, Euronews reported. Moscow had previously insisted that European representatives had no place at the negotiating table.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States had floated the idea of Ukraine ceding the Donbas region in return for NATO membership. Talks were reported to be heading to Abu Dhabi. An envoy also said Hungary is not blocking Ukraine's EU accession talks.
The fighting continues. Russian overnight attacks killed at least two people in Odesa and hit a hospital in Kyiv. Ukraine hit Russia's KINEF refinery, which handles about 7% of Russia's refining capacity, damaging three main processing units. These reports date from the past few days, and details may change.
levels.why: Any peace deal would decide Ukraine's borders and Europe's security, and affect energy prices and defence spending.

levels.headline: Russia drops insistence on shutting EU out of Ukraine talks as Kyiv says Donbas-for-NATO idea was floated
levels.body:
Moscow has softened its position and says it will not dictate whether EU delegates take part in Ukraine talks, having earlier said Europeans had no place at the table. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the US floated Ukraine giving up Donbas in return for NATO membership.
Talks were reported to be heading to Abu Dhabi, and an envoy said Hungary is not blocking Ukraine's accession talks with the EU.
On the battlefield, Russian attacks killed at least two people in Odesa and hit a hospital in Kyiv, while Ukraine damaged three main units at Russia's KINEF refinery, which handles about 7% of its refining capacity.
levels.why: The outcome will shape European security and the future of Ukraine's borders.

levels.headline: Russia is more flexible about EU involvement in Ukraine peace talks, as fighting goes on
levels.body:
Russia has changed its position on who can join peace talks over Ukraine. It had said European delegates had no place at the table. It now says it will not decide whether EU representatives take part. Meanwhile Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said that the US had floated a plan in which Ukraine would give up Donbas, an eastern region, in return for joining NATO.
Talks are reported to be heading to Abu Dhabi. A Ukrainian official said Hungary is not blocking Ukraine's progress towards EU membership.
The war goes on. Russian attacks killed at least two people in Odesa and hit a Kyiv hospital. Ukraine struck a major Russian oil refinery.
levels.why: The terms of any deal would affect safety in Europe and could change energy and defence costs.

levels.headline: Russia softens its line on the EU joining Ukraine peace talks
levels.body:
Russia has softened its position on who can take part in talks about ending the war in Ukraine. It had said that European countries should not be at the table. Now it says it will not decide whether EU delegates join.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the US had suggested that Ukraine could give up the eastern region of Donbas in return for being allowed to join NATO, the military alliance. The next talks were reported to be heading to Abu Dhabi.
The fighting has not stopped. Russian attacks killed at least two people in Odesa and hit a hospital in Kyiv. Ukraine hit one of Russia's oil refineries, damaging three main units.
levels.why: A peace deal would affect Ukraine's future and the safety of all of Europe.

levels.headline: Russia says it will not stop the EU joining peace talks about Ukraine
levels.body:
The war in Ukraine began when Russia invaded in 2022. Countries have been trying to agree peace. Russia had said the EU, a group of European countries, should not be part of the talks. Now it says it will not decide who is there.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the US suggested a trade. Ukraine would give up Donbas, a region in the east, and in return could join NATO, a group of countries that promise to help each other if attacked.
The talks are said to be moving to Abu Dhabi. But the fighting goes on. Russian attacks killed at least two people in Odesa and hit a hospital in Kyiv. Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery.
levels.why: Any deal will decide where Ukraine's borders are and how safe Europe feels.

levels.headline: Russia says it will not block the EU from Ukraine peace talks, and a Donbas-for-NATO idea has been floated
levels.body:
The war in Ukraine began when Russia invaded in 2022. Other countries have been trying to help the two sides agree peace. Russia had said that European countries should not be at the talks. Now it says it will not decide who takes part.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the US floated a swap. Ukraine would give up Donbas, a region in the east, and in return could join NATO, a group of countries that promise to defend each other. The next talks were reported to be heading to Abu Dhabi.
The fighting goes on. Russian attacks killed at least two people in Odesa and hit a hospital in Kyiv, and Ukraine damaged a Russian oil refinery.
levels.why: A deal would decide Ukraine's borders and how safe Europe feels.

levels.headline: Russia says the EU can join talks about the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine are at war. Other countries are trying to help them agree on peace. At first, Russia said countries of the European Union should not join the talks. Now it says it will not stop them.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the US had a new idea. Ukraine would give up a part of its land in the east, called Donbas. In return, it could join NATO. That is a group of countries that promise to protect each other.
The next talks may be in Abu Dhabi. But the war is still going on. People have been hurt in Odesa and Kyiv, and a hospital was hit. Ukraine hit an oil factory in Russia.
levels.why: The talks could decide whether the war stops and where the border will be.

levels.headline: Countries are still talking about how to stop the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
Russia is fighting a war against its neighbour, Ukraine. Other countries are trying to help them make peace. They are having meetings to talk about it.
Russia first said that countries from Europe could not come to the meetings. Now it says it will not say no.
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the US had a new idea. Ukraine would give up some land in the east. In return, it could join NATO. That is a group of countries that promise to look after each other.
But the war has not stopped. Some people were hurt in Odesa and Kyiv, including at a hospital. Ukraine hit an oil factory in Russia.
levels.why: The talks could help stop people being hurt and decide who owns the land.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are still trying to end a war in Ukraine
levels.body:
Imagine two groups of children have been fighting in the playground for a very long time. Teachers are trying to help them stop and make friends. This is a bit like what is happening with two countries, Russia and Ukraine.
The teachers are the leaders of other countries. They meet to talk about how to end the fighting. First Russia said some of the teachers could not come. Now it says that is fine.
Somebody has also suggested a swap. Ukraine would give up some land, and in return it would get a promise of protection from a big group of countries.
But the fighting has not stopped, and people have still been hurt.
levels.why: It is important that leaders talk, because war hurts many people.

levels.headline: Leaders are still trying to stop a war between two countries
levels.body:
Do you remember a time when two friends were really cross with each other? A grown-up might sit down with them and help them talk. That is what is happening with two countries called Russia and Ukraine. They are fighting a war.
The grown-ups are leaders of other countries. They are meeting to talk about how to stop the fight. Russia had said that some of them could not join. Now it says it does not mind.
Someone also had an idea for a swap that might help. But nobody has agreed yet. And sadly, people are still being hurt while they talk.
levels.why: When leaders talk instead of fight, fewer people get hurt.

headline: Representation of the People Bill, which would give 16 and 17-year-olds the vote in all elections, enters Lords committee stage

terms.meaning: The step where a bill is examined line by line and changes are proposed.
The UK's second chamber of Parliament, which checks and can amend laws.

levels.headline: Representation of the People Bill, which would give 16 and 17-year-olds the vote in all elections, enters Lords committee stage
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has entered its committee stage in the House of Lords, according to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. One of its main aims is to give 16 and 17-year-olds the vote in all elections.
Committee stage is the point where peers go through a bill line by line and can propose changes. It comes after the bill has been debated in principle and before further stages, and before it can become law the Commons and Lords must agree the final text.
Currently 18 is the minimum voting age for UK general elections, although 16 and 17-year-olds can vote in some elections in Scotland and Wales. The bill is one of several political stories in a week when attention also turns to the UK-EU summit on 20 November.
levels.why: The bill could change who can vote in elections and bring hundreds of thousands of young people into the electorate.

levels.headline: Votes at 16 bill reaches Lords committee stage
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill is now at committee stage in the House of Lords, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said. The bill would extend the vote to 16 and 17-year-olds in all elections.
At this stage peers examine the bill clause by clause and can table amendments. After later stages, both Houses have to agree the final wording before the bill can become law.
At present the minimum voting age for UK general elections is 18, although 16 and 17-year-olds can vote in some elections in Scotland and Wales.
levels.why: It could change the make-up of the electorate and how parties approach young voters.

levels.headline: A bill to give 16 and 17-year-olds the vote in all elections is being examined by the House of Lords
levels.body:
A bill that would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in all elections has reached the committee stage in the House of Lords. It is called the Representation of the People Bill. The government department for housing and communities announced it.
At committee stage, members of the Lords go through the bill line by line and can suggest changes. The bill must still pass later stages, and the Commons and Lords must agree the final text, before it can become law.
At the moment you must be 18 to vote in UK general elections. In Scotland and Wales, 16 and 17-year-olds can already vote in some elections.
levels.why: It could give a new group of young people a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: The House of Lords begins detailed examination of a bill to lower the voting age to 16
levels.body:
A bill to let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in all elections is being looked at in detail by the House of Lords. It is the Representation of the People Bill. This step is called committee stage.
At committee stage, members of the Lords study the bill line by line and can suggest changes. Both parts of Parliament, the Commons and the Lords, must agree on the final wording before the bill becomes law.
The minimum age for voting in UK general elections is now 18, though 16 and 17-year-olds can vote in some elections in Scotland and Wales. The bill would bring the same age in everywhere.
levels.why: If it passes, many more young people would be able to vote.

levels.headline: A bill to let 16 and 17-year-olds vote is being checked by the House of Lords
levels.body:
Parliament makes the laws in the UK. A new idea for a law is called a bill. This bill is called the Representation of the People Bill. It would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in every kind of election.
Now it is being checked by the House of Lords. This is one of the two parts of Parliament. The other is the House of Commons, where MPs sit. The Lords go through the bill line by line and can suggest changes. This part is called the committee stage.
Right now you must be 18 to vote in a general election. But in Scotland and Wales, some elections already let 16 and 17-year-olds vote.
levels.why: Lowering the voting age would let more young people have a say.

levels.headline: A new law that would let 16-year-olds vote is being checked in Parliament
levels.body:
In the UK, laws are made in Parliament. A new idea for a law is called a bill. This bill would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in all elections. Elections are when people choose who will run the country or the town.
Parliament has two parts. One is the House of Commons, and the other is the House of Lords. Both have to agree on a bill. Now the Lords are checking it carefully, line by line. They can suggest changes.
At the moment you have to be 18 to vote in a general election. In Scotland and Wales, young people can already vote at 16 in some elections.
levels.why: It would give more young people a say in who makes decisions.

levels.headline: Parliament is checking a plan to let 16-year-olds vote
levels.body:
Voting is when people choose who will make decisions for the country. At the moment you must be 18 to choose in the big national vote. A new plan would let 16 and 17-year-olds do it too.
A plan like this has to be checked by Parliament. Parliament has two parts. They are called the House of Commons and the House of Lords. The Lords are looking at the plan very carefully now. They go through it line by line and can suggest changes.
In Scotland and Wales, young people can already vote at 16 in some votes. If the plan becomes law, it would be the same everywhere.
levels.why: If the plan passes, many more teenagers will be able to vote.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are checking a plan to let teenagers vote
levels.body:
Voting is how people choose the leaders of a country. Right now you have to be 18 before you can vote in the big vote. A new plan says that 16 and 17-year-olds should be able to vote too.
Before a plan becomes a law, a group of grown-ups called the House of Lords must look at it very carefully. They read every line. They can say, I think we should change this bit.
If it becomes a law, teenagers would be able to help choose the leaders. Some places, like Scotland and Wales, already let 16-year-olds vote in some votes.
levels.why: It would let more young people help choose who leads the country.

levels.headline: A plan to let teenagers help choose leaders is being checked
levels.body:
Do you have a class vote for who should be class helper? Everyone puts up a hand. That is a kind of voting. Grown-ups vote too, to choose who will lead the country.
At the moment, you have to be 18 to vote in the big vote. A new plan says that 16 and 17-year-olds could vote too.
Before a plan can become a rule, some very important grown-ups, called the House of Lords, check it very carefully. They read it line by line. They may say, let us change that bit.
If it passes, more teenagers will help choose the leaders.
levels.why: Voting is a way for people to have a say, even when they are young.

levels.headline: A rule about voting is being checked
levels.body:
Do you remember voting for something in class, like which game to play? Everyone had a say. Grown-ups vote too, to choose who will help look after the country.
Right now, you have to be 18 to vote in the big vote. A new plan says that teenagers who are 16 could vote too.
Before a plan becomes a rule, some grown-ups have to check it carefully. They are called the House of Lords. They read every line. They may want to change a few words.
If the plan passes, teenagers who are older than you would get to have a say too.
levels.why: Voting lets people have a say in how their country is run.
